description: National AI ethics boards in multiple member states begin issuing conflicting rulings on high-risk systems, creating legal uncertainty for cross-border deployment. This divergence emerges as trust in EU-level coordination collapses and national governments assert sovereign oversight in response to public pressure and repeated institutional failures.

Following a series of unattributed attacks on Nordic and Benelux infrastructure, a loose coalition of EU and non-EU European states forms an informal mutual assistance pact for AI-driven cyber defence, sharing threat models and automated countermeasures in real time. The arrangement operates outside formal EU channels, reflecting deepening distrust in centralised resilience planning.

Decentralized collectives of researchers, municipal IT departments, and open-source developers across the EU begin federating their infrastructure and models into a shared, resilient network outside official channels. This grassroots alternative to state-led AI infrastructure gains traction amid collapsing trust in public institutions and demonstrates early success in local service automation.

A cascade of AI-driven logistics failures in East Asia, originating from an unreported loss-of-control incident at a major shipping consortium, disrupts global semiconductor supply chains. The EU experiences sudden delays in receiving critical components for data centres and edge devices, amplifying existing sovereignty concerns and exposing fragility in supposedly diversified supply routes.

Leading researchers in multiple frontier labs report a breakdown in peer review and reproducibility as AI-generated papers flood publication pipelines, with models increasingly citing non-existent studies. Journals begin retracting dozens of articles, and major conferences impose emergency AI-authentication requirements. This cascades into public skepticism about all AI-assisted research outputs, including those underpinning policy decisions in the EU.

A coalition of Global South nations forms the 'Equitable AI Front', demanding binding international access to open-weight models above capability 60 and technology transfer mechanisms. They cite the EU's dependency crisis as proof that even wealthy regions cannot secure autonomy under current governance, and leverage growing voting power in UN agencies to push for reforms. This creates diplomatic pressure on both the US and EU to engage, despite resistance from leading AI states.
